title: NEB Class 11 Biology — Evolutionary Biology — 2024
subject: biology
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Explain Darwin's theory of natural selection with an example.
questions.solution:
**Darwin (1859):** overproduction → variation → struggle for existence → survival of the fittest → inheritance of favourable traits → new species over time.

**Example — industrial melanism:** soot-darkened trees hid dark peppered moths from birds while pale ones were eaten; dark alleles spread until clean-air laws reversed the trend — selection observed in decades.
questions.knowledgeNote: 'Descent with modification' plus genetics became the modern synthesis — Darwin's mechanism, Mendel's inheritance.
questions.answer: **Darwin's theory of natural selection:** (1) **overproduction** — far more offspring are born than survive; (2) **struggle for existence** — competition for limited food, space and mates; (3) **variation** — individuals differ in inherited traits; (4) **natural selection (survival of the fittest)** — the best-adapted variants survive and reproduce disproportionately; (5) **speciation** — favourable variations accumulate over generations, producing new species. **Example — industrial melanism:** in pre-industrial England the pale peppered moth (*Biston betularia*) matched lichen-covered trunks and the rare dark mutant was eaten; in soot-blackened industrial cities the dark form was the camouflaged one and rose to ~95% of populations; with pollution control the pale form returned — differential survival by birds is natural selection recorded in real time. **Deep point:** selection edits variation, it never writes it — the dark mutant existed before the smoke; the environment only decided which allele would win.

questions.question: What are the evidences of evolution? Explain with one example each from morphological and paleontological studies.
questions.solution:
**Morphological:** homologous structures — same bone plan, different jobs (human arm, whale flipper, bat wing prove common ancestry).

**Paleontological:** fossils ordered simple→complex in strata; **Archaeopteryx** bridges reptiles and birds (teeth and claws with feathers).
questions.knowledgeNote: Homologous = shared ancestry; analogous (bird vs insect wings) = convergent function, different origin.
questions.answer: **Evidences of evolution:** fossils; homologous and analogous organs; vestigial organs; embryology; connecting links; biogeography; molecular/biochemical uniformity (DNA code). **Morphological evidence — homologous organs:** same structure, different function — the **pentadactyl forelimb** of man (grasping), bat (flight), whale (swimming), horse (running) shares the same bone plan, betraying a common ancestor with divergent evolution. **Palaeontological evidence — fossils:** the fossil record preserved in chronological rock strata — **Archaeopteryx** (reptilian teeth/tail + avian feathers) as the reptile–bird connecting link, and the graded horse series Eohippus → Merychippus → Equus showing gradual evolution in time. **Deep point:** anatomy shows the relationship, fossils show the timetable — the two evidences independently agree, which is what makes the case overwhelming.

questions.question: Compare Lamarck's and Darwin's theories of evolution.
questions.solution:
**Lamarck:** use and disuse develops organs; acquired characters are inherited (giraffe stretching its neck).

**Darwin:** variation already exists; nature selects the fittest, and only germ-line traits pass on.

Lamarck fails because acquired changes (a blacksmith's muscles) are not inherited — Weismann's mouse-tail experiments disproved it.
questions.knowledgeNote: Lamarck = inheritance of acquired characters; Darwin = selection on variation — one line each settles the comparison.
questions.answer: **Lamarck vs Darwin:** **Lamarck (inheritance of acquired characters):** (1) organisms **change because the environment changes** — new needs arise; (2) **use and disuse** — organs used more develop, unused ones weaken (giraffe stretched its neck reaching leaves); (3) **acquired characters are inherited** — the stretched neck passes to offspring. **Darwin (natural selection):** (1) **variation exists spontaneously and heritably** before the environment acts; (2) the environment **selects** — individuals already born with longer necks reach more food, survive and breed better; (3) **no inheritance of acquired characters** — only inherited variation matters; evolution is differential survival, not striving. **Key differences:** cause of change (environment-induced striving vs pre-existing variation selected); mechanism of inheritance (acquired traits inherited vs only germ-line variation inherited); direction (goal-directed vs undirected, opportunistic). **Verdict:** Darwin's mechanism is supported by genetics (Weismann's mouse-tail amputation experiment showed acquired characters are not inherited); Lamarck is remembered for recognising evolution and adaptation, but his mechanism failed. **Deep point:** the giraffe settles the argument — for Lamarck it *stretched*, for Darwin it was *born* with a longer neck and outlived its shorter-necked cousins; modern genetics sides with Darwin, with a footnote that epigenetics gives Lamarck a small posthumous consolation.

questions.question: State the Hardy-Weinberg principle. List the factors that disturb genetic equilibrium.
questions.solution:
**Principle:** allele frequencies (p + q = 1; p² + 2pq + q² = 1) stay constant generation after generation in an ideal population.

**Disturbers:** mutation, selection, migration (gene flow), genetic drift (small populations), and non-random mating.
questions.knowledgeNote: The equation is the null hypothesis of evolution — deviation from it MEASURES evolution happening.
questions.answer: **Hardy–Weinberg principle:** in a **large, randomly mating population free from evolutionary forces**, allele and genotype frequencies remain **constant from generation to generation** — genetic equilibrium. For two alleles A (p) and a (q): **p + q = 1**, and the genotype frequencies are **p² + 2pq + q² = 1** (AA : Aa : aa). **Factors that disturb the equilibrium (evolutionary forces):** (1) **mutation** — creates new alleles; (2) **gene flow (migration)** — alleles move between populations; (3) **genetic drift** — random chance changes in small populations (founder effect, bottleneck); (4) **natural selection** — differential survival of genotypes; (5) **non-random mating** — assortative/inbreeding shifts genotype frequencies. **Deep point:** the equation is evolution's null hypothesis — a population sitting on p² + 2pq + q² is *not* evolving; any measured deviation names the force at work.

questions.question: Distinguish between homologous and analogous organs with one example of each.
questions.solution:
**Homologous:** same origin/structure, different functions — e.g. human forelimb vs bat wing (divergent evolution, common ancestry).

**Analogous:** different origins, same function — e.g. butterfly vs bird wings (convergent evolution, no close ancestry).
questions.knowledgeNote: Vestigial organs (human appendix, whale pelvis) are homology's leftovers — reduced structures proving past function.
questions.answer: **Homologous organs:** same basic structure and embryonic origin, **different functions**  — e.g. the forelimb of a man (grasping) and the wing of a bat (flying) share the same pentadactyl bone plan ⟹ common ancestry (divergent evolution). **Analogous organs:** different structures and origins, **same function** — e.g. the wing of a bird (modified forelimb) and the wing of an insect (fold of exoskeleton) both fly ⟹ convergent evolution. **Deep point:** homology is shared ancestry wearing different jobs; analogy is the same job invented twice — only homology testifies to descent.

questions.question: Outline the stages of human evolution from Dryopithecus to Homo sapiens.
questions.solution: **Dryopithecus** (ape-like, Miocene) → **Ramapithecus** (early hominid) → **Australopithecus** (bipedal, small brain) → **H. habilis** (tool maker) → **H. erectus** (fire, larger brain) → **Neanderthals** (burials) → **H. sapiens** (modern, Cro-Magnon art).
questions.knowledgeNote: Bipedalism came before brain expansion — walking upright freed the hands millions of years before wit followed.
questions.answer: **Stages of human evolution (Dryopithecus → Homo sapiens):** **(1) Dryopithecus (~15–20 Mya, Miocene):** ape-like, arboreal, knuckle-walker — the common ancestor stock of apes and man. **(2) Ramapithecus (~12–14 Mya):** first ape-man; thick jaws, semi-erect; lived in open country. **(3) Australopithecus (~2–4 Mya, 'Lucy', A. africanus):** **first true biped** — upright walking, small brain (~450–600 cc), omnivorous tool use (pebble tools). **(4) Homo habilis (~1.5–2 Mya):** 'handy man' — first **stone tool maker**, brain ~700 cc, still partly arboreal. **(5) Homo erectus (~0.5–1.5 Mya, Java/Peking man):** fully erect, larger brain (~900–1100 cc), **fire and hunting**, first to leave Africa. **(6) Homo sapiens neanderthalensis (~40–100 thousand yr):** heavy build, large brain (~1400 cc), buried their dead, primitive social life. **(7) Homo sapiens sapiens (~10–50 thousand yr, Cro-Magnon):** modern man — brain ~1400–1600 cc, upright, articulate speech, cave art, agriculture and civilisation. **Deep point:** the trend line is bipedalism first, then brain, then culture — walking freed the hands, the hands made tools, the tools fed the brain.
